scenes.name: El pop de papá y mamá
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los adultos compraban LPs (a 32 chelines frente a los 6 de un single) y también muchos singles, de modo que la lista británica de 1965 era esquizofrénica: los Stones y los Beatles competían con lo que los adolescentes llamaban «música de papás y mamás», Ken Dodd, los Seekers, los Bachelors o Jim Reeves. La banda sonora de The Sound of Music encabezó la lista de LPs casi todo 1965 y 1966. Los adolescentes más jóvenes encontraban nuevos ídolos como los Walker Brothers, baladistas melodramáticos a lo Spector.
scenes.family: Pop de estudio: Spector, Beach Boys, Meek

scenes.name: Contracultura: cantautores eléctricos
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La fusión de música y política convierte el rock en vehículo de la disidencia: la contracultura. Todo empieza con Bob Dylan, el músico más influyente de los sesenta, que redefine el rock como composición metafísica y libre (Highway 61 Revisited, Blonde On Blonde). La transición del folk-singer al cantautor eléctrico abre infinitas vías: Fred Neil, Tim Hardin, Neil Diamond, Paul Simon (el poeta del chico tímido y solitario), Donovan (la quintaesencia del ideal hippy) y Country Joe McDonald, agit-prop de Berkeley.

scenes.name: Reggae y dub
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El reggae se populariza en el Reino Unido con Prince Buster y Desmond Dekker; Jimmy Cliff lo casa con el «paz y amor» hippy y los Maytals le dan nombre. Los sound systems de los guetos convierten a los «selectors» en los verdaderos animadores: el «toasting» sobre los discos será tan importante como la música. Bob Marley y los Wailers lo llevan a Occidente; Burning Spear firma quizá su cima artística (Marcus Garvey). Los ingenieros remezclan las caras B quitando las voces: King Tubby inventa el dub usando la mesa de mezclas como un instrumento, y Lee Perry (Super Ape) y Augustus Pablo fijan el canon.
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

podcast.title: Strategic Hiatus (1972-1976)
podcast.body: Neil Diamond deliberately stayed off the stage for four years between 1972 and 1976, aiming to learn from the experiences of artists like Elvis Presley and The Beatles. He believed that constant public presence could lead to an artist becoming "public property" and wished to maintain his independence. "He actually said he tried to learn a little something from Elvis and the Beatles. He said, I think if you're out in front of the public too much, if you're too recognized, too well known, you do in a sense become public property. I always wanted to be my own man."

podcast.body: Albums by Neil Diamond were among those shipped with the Sony BMG Rootkit malware (XCP and MediaMax) installed. This software was surreptitiously placed on users' computers when they attempted to rip CDs, compromising system security without their consent. "The XCP malware came on albums ranging from Neil Diamond to Frank Sinatra to Celine Dion to Cindy Lopper."

podcast.title: Creative Control and Urge to Write
podcast.body: Upon signing with UNI, the same label as Elton John, Neil Diamond gained significantly more control over his songwriting. He described his urge to write as an "uncontrollable force," wishing he could write only when he felt like it, at his own pace. "At UNI, the label that also signed Elton John, he had a lot more control over what he wrote, which was almost kind of like this uncontrollable force in him."

podcast.title: Early Career Path and Influences
podcast.body: Neil Diamond's parents had hoped he would become a doctor, but he ultimately pursued music, initially assuming he would be a songwriter. His inspiration for songwriting came from the folk legend Pete Seeger. "When it became clear that he was going to go into music rather than be a doctor, which his parents would have preferred, he assumed it would be as a songwriter. His inspiration came from the folk legend Peepseger."

podcast.title: Introducing Elton John at The Troubadour
podcast.body: Two months after recording his own live album "Neil Diamond Gold" at The Troubadour in July 1970, Neil Diamond returned to the venue. He took the stage to introduce his new British rock singer and UNI record label mate, Elton John, who was making his American debut that night. "Two months after recording Neil Diamond Gold, the record that was recorded at the Trubidor, he returned to the Trubidor to introduce a new British rock singer and a UNI record label mate who was making his American debut at the Trubidor."

podcast.title: Struggling Songwriter to Hitmaker
podcast.body: For about eight years, Diamond made only around $20 a year in royalties as a songwriter, forcing him to sell vitamin pills door-to-door to support himself. His financial situation changed significantly after Jay and the Americans recorded "Sunday and Me" in 1966, providing him with enough money to enter a recording studio and record his own three hit singles. "He made about 20 bucks a year in royalties. And he had to do things like sell vitamin pills, door to door to make money to do things like eat."

podcast.title: The "Jewish Elvis"
podcast.body: Neil Diamond was sometimes referred to as the "Jewish Elvis" due to his looks and commanding stage persona. A key difference highlighted is that Diamond was a prolific songwriter, a role Elvis Presley never fulfilled. "Neil Diamond was called by some, the Jewish Elvis, because of his looks and because of his stage persona."

podcast.title: Zero DB Initiative Signatory
podcast.body: Neil Diamond is among the artists who signed the Zero DB initiative, established in 2008 by the charity Reprieve. This initiative encourages condemnation of music as torture and advocates for governments to enforce international treaties related to prisoner treatment, such as the Convention Against Torture. "The Sinees include Tom Morello, average against the machine, members of REM, rise against Pearl Jam, Trent Reznor, Limp Biscuit, system of a down, disturbed the estate of Prince, the Chili Peppers, Eminem, Marilyn Manson, Neil Diamond, Dr. Dre, and a host of others."

xref.title: Blackie O'Nassis Death (June 13, 2023) – Drummer on Pulp Fiction's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon"; Age 57, Cause Unknown
xref.body: John Rowan, who played under the name Blackie O'Nassis, was the drummer for Urge Overkill — the Chicago band whose cover of Neil Diamond's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon" (1967) appears in the famous dance scene in *Pulp Fiction*. The band was also a cult favorite in the alt-rock community and opened for Nirvana on the *Nevermind* tour, during which they befriended Kurt Cobain, Chrissie Hynde of the Pretenders, and Liz Phair. Blackie left the band in 1996; there were reports of heroin use and at least one arrest. The cause of his death on June 13, 2023, at age 57 was never disclosed. "As for the cause of his death on June 13th, 2023, we have no idea."

xref.title: Estate as Zero DB Initiative Signatory
xref.body: The estate of Prince is among the signatories of the Zero DB initiative, formed in 2008 by the charity Reprieve. This initiative encourages condemnation of music as torture and advocates for governments to enforce the Convention Against Torture and other treaties concerning prisoner treatment. "The Sinees include Tom Morello, average against the machine, members of REM, rise against Pearl Jam, Trent Reznor, Limp Biscuit, system of a down, disturbed the estate of Prince, the Chili Peppers, Eminem, Marilyn Manson, Neil Diamond, Dr. Dre, and a host of others."
